text: react-virtualized is a collection of React components for efficiently rendering large lists and tabular data. Only the rows and columns visible within the viewport are rendered, which keeps the number of DOM elements small no matter how much data there is. If you're starting a new project, also take a look at react-window as a lighter-weight alternative. Installation Begin by installing the library from NPM: TypeScript definitions are included within the published dist folder. Support Here are some ways to support this project: Become a GitHub sponsor Buy me a coffee

headings.title: Controlled mode
headings.text: Controlled mode By default, ArrowKeyStepper manages the current scrollToColumn and scrollToRow values itself (the props of the same name only set their initial values). To manage them yourself, e.g. to also select a cell by clicking it, set isControlled and update the values in response to onScrollToChange. The registered child is scrolled whenever the controlled values change. Click a cell below, then use the arrow keys: Arrow-key stepping can be turned off with the disabled prop. An uncontrolled stepper's current values can also be overridden imperatively, through a ref (see methods below).

text: ArrowKeyStepper decorates a virtualized component (such as a Grid, List, or Table) and responds to arrow-key events by scrolling one row or column at a time. This provides a snap-to behavior rather than the default browser scrolling behavior. Click inside the grid below to focus it, then use the up, down, left, and right arrow keys to move around: mode: "edges" (default) mode: "cells" ArrowKeyStepper uses a render function as its children. Pass the onSectionRendered parameter through to the decorated component (it informs the stepper which range of cells is currently visible) and attach the registerChild parameter as its ref; whenever the active cell changes, the stepper scrolls it into view by calling the component's scrollToCell method. The scrollToColumn and scrollToRow parameters identify the active cell, e.g. to highlight it. The mode prop controls how the stepper behaves when an arrow key is pressed: in "edges" mode (the default), the next row or column beyond the visible edge of the grid is scrolled into view; in "cells" mode, the current row or column index is only incremented or decremented by 1. Unlike the other HOCs in react-virtualized, ArrowKeyStepper adds a <div> element around its children in order to attach a key-down event handler. The appearance of this wrapper element can be customized using the className property.
title: ArrowKeyStepper

headings.title: Dynamic row heights
headings.text: Dynamic row heights The most common use case is a List whose rows contain wrapping text. Each row is rendered at the width of the list and its height is measured: Three pieces work together to make this work: A CellMeasurerCache stores the measurements. It's configured with fixedWidth: true since only heights are measured. Each row is wrapped in a CellMeasurer, which is passed the cache along with the row's index and the parent provided to the row renderer. The cache is passed to the List as deferredMeasurementCache, and its rowHeight method is used as the rowHeight prop. CellMeasurer attaches a ref to its child in order to find the DOM element to measure, so the child should be a DOM element (or a component that passes its ref along to one; see child requirements). The style passed to the row (or cell) renderer must still be applied to the element, in order to position it. Measurements depend on the available width when text wraps. When the width changes (e.g. on window resize), call cache.clearAll() so that cells get re-measured, as the examples on this page do in the AutoSizer onResize callback.

headings.title: Function children: measure and registerChild
headings.text: Function children: measure and registerChild Instead of an element, CellMeasurer also accepts a function child. The function receives two parameters: measure: re-measures the cell. Call this when the cell's content is ready, or has changed size, after the initial render (for example when an image finishes loading). Calling it after the cell has unmounted (e.g. it scrolled out of view before the image loaded) does nothing. Both functions are stable. registerChild: specifies the DOM element to measure; it can be used as a ref. A registered element takes precedence over the element returned by the function. This example shows a List of images whose row heights can't be known until the image data has loaded:

headings.title: Child requirements
headings.text: Child requirements CellMeasurer measures the DOM element its ref is attached to. (If the child element has a ref of its own, that ref still receives the element.) The child can be: A DOM element, e.g. <div style={style}>. A function component that passes its ref along to a DOM element. In React 19, ref is a regular prop that can be passed to the element; in React 18, the component must use forwardRef. Anything else (e.g. a component that doesn't pass its ref along, a class component, or a fragment), as long as a function child passes registerChild to the element to be measured. An element registered with registerChild takes precedence over the child element, so it can also be used to measure an element nested within the child. If there is no DOM element to measure (e.g. the child is text, an array or a fragment, or a component that doesn't pass its ref along), the child is rendered as-is, the cell keeps the cache's default size, and a warning is logged in development mode.

text: CellMeasurer is a higher-order component that automatically measures a cell's contents just-in-time, e.g. for messages in a chat interface whose size isn't known until they've been rendered. Specify a fixed width to measure dynamic height (or vice versa). CellMeasurer can be used with Grid, List, Table, MultiGrid, and Masonry. If sizes can be determined ahead of time (e.g. from the data), it's simpler and more efficient to pass a rowHeight or columnWidth function than to measure cells; see variable row heights and variable sizes. Use CellMeasurer when a cell's size depends on its rendered content (e.g. wrapping text or images). This is an advanced component, with some limitations and performance considerations; see limitations and performance.

text: Measuring a column's width requires measuring all of the rows in order to determine the widest occurrence of that column. The same is true in reverse for measuring a row's height. For this reason it may not be a good idea to use CellMeasurer for Grids containing a large number of both columns and rows. (This is also why a CellMeasurerCache should be configured with either fixedWidth or fixedHeight.) Since cells are measured one at a time as they are rendered, performance can suffer if a user skips many rows (or columns) at once, by dragging the scrollbar or by calling a method like scrollToCell or scrollToRow. There is (unfortunately) no workaround for this limitation at the moment. If sizes can be determined ahead of time (e.g. from the data), it's more efficient to pass a rowHeight or columnWidth function than to measure cells.

headings.title: How do I upgrade from version 9?
headings.text: How do I upgrade from version 9? Version 10 requires React 18 or newer, removes a few components (AutoSizer, Collection and WindowScroller), and replaces the controlled scroll props (e.g. scrollToIndex) with methods. The migration guide in the changelog covers each change, with before/after examples.

headings.title: Why is nothing rendered (or why does AutoSizer report a height of 0)?
headings.text: Why is nothing rendered (or why does AutoSizer report a height of 0)? List, Grid, Table, and Masonry need an explicit height and width (only a width when they are scrolled by the window). AutoSizer (from the react-virtualized-auto-sizer package) can provide them, but it only fills its parent; it won't stretch it. If the parent (or one of its ancestors) has no height, AutoSizer reports 0 and nothing is rendered. Give the parent a size (e.g. height: 100% or flex: 1); inside a flex container, wrap AutoSizer in a div with flex: 1 1 auto. See sizing components for more.

headings.title: How do I scroll to a row (or cell)?
headings.text: How do I scroll to a row (or cell)? Call scrollToRow({ index, align }) on a List or Table, or scrollToCell({ columnIndex, rowIndex, align }) on a Grid, through a ref. In version 10, these methods replace the scrollToIndex and scrollToRow props. They scroll once: the row isn't kept in view if sizes change afterwards, so to scroll to a row that is being added, call them once it has rendered (e.g. in an effect). To render a list at a scroll position from the start (e.g. when restoring it), use the initialScrollTop prop instead.

headings.title: How do I make a list scroll with the rest of the page?
headings.text: How do I make a list scroll with the rest of the page? Set the scrollElement prop of a List, Grid, Table or Masonry to "window" (or to a scrollable element). The component then renders at its full height, renders only the rows visible within the window, and its scroll methods scroll the window; it only needs a width. In version 10, this replaces WindowScroller. See window scrolling.

headings.title: Why do my Table and other components look unstyled?
headings.text: Why do my Table and other components look unstyled? react-virtualized ships a small set of default styles that must be imported once, e.g. when your application starts: import "react-virtualized/styles.css";. You can also skip them and provide your own; see customizing styles.

headings.title: Why doesn't my list update when my data changes?
headings.text: Why doesn't my list update when my data changes? The components only re-render when their props change (shallow comparison). If your data changes but props like rowCount don't (e.g. after re-sorting), either pass the changed value through as an extra prop (e.g. sortBy={sortBy}) or force an update: forceUpdateGrid() for List and Table, forceUpdate() for Grid and Masonry.

headings.title: My row heights (or column widths) changed. Why is the layout stale?
headings.text: My row heights (or column widths) changed. Why is the layout stale? Sizes are cached once they have been computed, because the components only know rowCount/columnCount and can't tell when the underlying data changes. Call recomputeRowHeights(index) on List or Table, or recomputeGridSize({ columnIndex, rowIndex }) on Grid, starting from the first index whose size changed. (This is only needed when sizes come from a function; changes to a numeric rowHeight or columnWidth are applied automatically.)

headings.title: When should I clear a CellMeasurerCache?
headings.text: When should I clear a CellMeasurerCache? CellMeasurer measures each cell once and caches the result. Call cache.clear(rowIndex, columnIndex) when a cell's content changes (e.g. a loading indicator is replaced with content), and cache.clearAll() when all cells need to reflow (e.g. the width changed and text wraps differently); then tell the parent to recompute its sizes (recomputeRowHeights() on a List or Table, recomputeGridSize() on a Grid). See CellMeasurerCache. If items can be added, removed, or re-ordered, pass a keyMapper (e.g. mapping indices to item IDs) so cached sizes follow the items rather than their indices.

headings.title: Can CellMeasurer measure both widths and heights?
headings.text: Can CellMeasurer measure both widths and heights? Not efficiently: a row's height is the tallest cell in that row (and a column's width is the widest cell in that column), so measuring requires rendering every cell in it. Use fixedWidth or fixedHeight on the CellMeasurerCache to measure only one dimension. Measuring can also be slow when users jump far ahead with the scrollbar, so provide sizes up front when you can.

headings.title: Should I use react-virtualized or react-window?
headings.text: Should I use react-virtualized or react-window? react-window is a smaller, lighter-weight library by the same author, with a simpler API, and is a good choice for new projects that need a list or grid. react-virtualized offers more components (e.g. Table, Masonry, MultiGrid, CellMeasurer, and InfiniteLoader), and version 10 keeps existing applications working on modern React.

headings.title: Rendering cells
headings.text: Rendering cells The cellRenderer function is responsible for rendering a single cell, given its row and column index. It receives the following parameters: The style parameter must be applied to the rendered cell; it specifies how the cell is sized and positioned, and the grid depends on it to scroll correctly. Don't modify the style object (it is cached and re-used by the grid); create a new object if you need to add style properties. Rows and columns don't all need to be the same size; see variable sizes. Grid supports the following static class names, in addition to the className, id, and style props (and containerStyle for the inner container): ReactVirtualized__Grid: main (outer) element ReactVirtualized__Grid__innerScrollContainer: inner scrollable area See customizing styles for more information.

text: Grid renders tabular data with virtualization along both the vertical and horizontal axes. Only the cells needed to fill the grid (based on its current horizontal and vertical scroll position) are rendered. To render a grid, specify its size (width and height), the number of rows and columns (rowCount and columnCount), the size of each (rowHeight and columnWidth), and a function that renders a cell (cellRenderer). The example above uses AutoSizer to fill the available space: Grid is also the building block for the other components in this library; List, Table, and MultiGrid all render a Grid internally. See Grid props and Grid methods for the full API.
title: Rendering a grid

headings.title: Parameters
headings.text: Parameters The cellRangeRenderer function receives the following parameters. If you require greater customization, you may want to fork defaultCellRangeRenderer and use them to render cells yourself. cellCache, styleCache: temporary cell and style caches used while scrolling cellRenderer: the cellRenderer prop supplied to the grid columnStartIndex, columnStopIndex, rowStartIndex, rowStopIndex: indices of the first and last columns and rows (inclusive) to render, including overscanned cells visibleColumnIndices, visibleRowIndices: the range of visible (not overscanned) columns and rows columnSizeAndPositionManager, rowSizeAndPositionManager: their getSizeAndPositionOfCell(index) method returns the offset (left or top) and size (width or height) of a column or row horizontalOffsetAdjustment, verticalOffsetAdjustment: pixel offsets to add to cell positions. Browsers limit the size of an element, so for very large grids, cell offsets are scaled down and cells are shifted as the user scrolls. isScrolling: the grid is currently being scrolled; isScrollingOptOut: the value of the grid prop scrollLeft, scrollTop: the current scroll offsets of the grid deferredMeasurementCache: the CellMeasurer cache, if one was passed to the grid parent: the grid instance (or the component that wraps it) Each rendered element needs a unique key. Cell positions must include the offset adjustments; otherwise cells will be mispositioned in very large grids.

text: The cellRangeRenderer prop is an advanced property, responsible for rendering the group of cells within a range of row and column indices. It is useful for situations where the grid requires additional, overlaid UI, such as a Gantt chart or a calendar application. Many use cases can be solved more easily using the onScroll callback or the ScrollSync component. If you do want to override cellRangeRenderer, the easiest way is to decorate the defaultCellRangeRenderer function (exported by the library) and add your own elements to the array it returns. Elements are positioned within the grid's inner scrollable container:
title: Custom cell range rendering

text: MultiGrid decorates Grid and adds fixed columns and/or rows. This is already possible using ScrollSync and two or more Grids, but MultiGrid reduces the boilerplate. Fixed columns Fixed rows MultiGrid accepts most of the Grid props. The majority of them (e.g. cellRenderer) are relayed to all of the child Grids, while some (e.g. columnCount and rowCount) are adjusted slightly to support fixed rows and columns. Row and column indices passed to cellRenderer (and to columnWidth and rowHeight functions) are always relative to the full grid, including the fixed rows and columns, and the parent passed to cellRenderer is the MultiGrid itself (so it can be passed to CellMeasurer as-is). A MultiGrid always scrolls itself, so (unlike Grid) it has no scrollElement prop and can't be scrolled by the window. Each of the four inner Grids (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right) can be styled separately using the className*Grid and style*Grid props listed (see MultiGrid props). Use enableFixedColumnScroll and enableFixedRowScroll to allow the user to scroll (e.g. with a mouse wheel) while the cursor is over the fixed column or row. The extra scrollbars this adds can be hidden with hideBottomLeftGridScrollbar and hideTopRightGridScrollbar. MultiGrid also works with CellMeasurer to measure dynamic column widths or row heights. To scroll a MultiGrid, call its scrollToCell or scrollToPosition methods through a ref; the fixed rows and columns are kept in sync with the scrollable section.
title: Fixed rows and columns

Typically cells are only measured as needed and estimated sizes are used for cells that have not yet been measured.
This method ensures that the next call to getTotalSize() returns an exact size (as opposed to just an estimated one).

headings.title: recomputeGridSize
headings.text:
recomputeGridSize Recomputes row heights and column widths after the specified index (both default to 0).
This function should be called if dynamic column or row sizes have changed but nothing else has.
Since Grid only receives columnCount and rowCount it has no way of detecting when the underlying data changes.
This method will also force a render cycle to ensure that the updated measurements are reflected in the rendered grid.

headings.title: scrollToCell
headings.text:
scrollToCell Ensure the specified column and/or row is visible (scrolling if necessary).
This method can be used to safely scroll back to a cell that a user has scrolled away from even if it was previously scrolled to.
The align parameter (default "auto") controls the alignment of the cell:
"auto" scrolls the least amount possible to ensure that the specified cell is fully visible
(a cell larger than the Grid is aligned to its start, so that its start is visible);
"start" aligns the cell to the top/left of the Grid and "end" to the bottom/right;
"center" aligns the cell in the middle of the Grid.
This is a one-time scroll: the cell is not kept in view afterwards (e.g. if the Grid's size or its cell sizes change).
Cells that haven't been measured yet (e.g. by CellMeasurer) are positioned using their estimated sizes.
Nothing is scrolled while the Grid's width or height is 0.
The column is ignored for single-column grids (e.g. List, Table).
If the Grid has a scrollElement, the scroll element (e.g. the window) is scrolled vertically instead.

headings.title: scrollToPosition
headings.text:
scrollToPosition Scroll to the specified offset(s); an omitted offset is left unchanged.
Offsets are clamped to the scrollable range.
Calling this method with the current offsets does nothing.
If the Grid has a scrollElement, scrollTop scrolls the scroll element (e.g. the window) instead
(to the position at which the Grid is scrolled by scrollTop).

headings.title: Choosing a value
headings.text: Choosing a value Overscanning has performance implications: the higher the value, the more cells need to be rendered in reaction to each scroll event. (See this slide for a visual example of how windowing works.) Setting an overscan value too high will erase the performance gains achieved by virtualization. Use the default value (10 rows) as a starting point and lower it if possible; aim for the lowest value that still generally avoids empty space appearing during normal scrolling. The same advice applies to overscanColumnCount. Consider tuning these values when: Cells are expensive to render: lower the overscan count so that less work is done per scroll event (and consider rendering a light-weight placeholder using the isScrolling parameter). Cells are cheap to render but blank space appears while scrolling quickly: raise the overscan count a little. A grid scrolls horizontally: overscanColumnCount defaults to 0, so a small value may help with horizontal scrolling.

headings.title: Custom overscan behavior
headings.text: Custom overscan behavior Which cells are overscanned is determined by the overscanIndicesGetter prop, an advanced property that calculates the range of cells to render before and after the visible range, along one axis at a time (it is called once for rows and once for columns). By default (defaultOverscanIndicesGetter), cells are only overscanned in the direction the user is scrolling, which is where content will be needed next. The library also exports an accessibilityOverscanIndicesGetter, which always renders at least one extra cell in both directions. This is necessary to support keyboard navigation (Tab / Shift+Tab) between cells in some cases. You can also provide your own function; for example, this one overscans the same number of cells in both directions (it is the "custom" option in the demo above): The function returns an object with the (inclusive) overscanStartIndex and overscanStopIndex of the cells to render. Make sure the returned range stays within 0 and cellCount - 1.

text: Virtualized components only render the rows and columns that are visible. "Overscanning" means rendering a few additional rows or columns just outside of the visible area, so that they are already in place when the user scrolls to them. This reduces the chance of a user scrolling faster than virtualized content can be rendered, which would briefly show empty space (or cause flickering on certain browsers and devices). See this slide for a visual example of why overscanning exists. Grid (and the components built on top of it, like List and Table) supports two overscan props: overscanRowCount: the number of rows to render above/below the visible rows; defaults to 10 overscanColumnCount: the number of columns to render before/after the visible columns; defaults to 0 By default, extra cells are only rendered in the direction the user is scrolling (e.g. below the visible rows when scrolling down), since that is where content will be needed next. Scroll the grid below to see the range of rendered rows change: defaultOverscanIndicesGetter
title: Overscan

Number of columns to render before/after the visible slice of the grid.
This can help reduce flickering during scrolling on certain browsers/devices.

The default value (10) is a good starting point; lower it if possible.

Element that scrolls the Grid (instead of the Grid scrolling itself): "window", or a scrollable DOM element
(e.g. a container that the Grid is rendered within, along with other content).
 The Grid then renders at its full height (it may still scroll horizontally itself), renders only the rows visible within the scroll element's viewport,
and its scroll methods scroll the scroll element.
Its position within the scroll element is measured when the scroll element scrolls or is resized, and when the Grid re-renders
(e.g. call forceUpdate() if content above the Grid changes size without the Grid re-rendering).
Pass null while the scroll element isn't available yet (e.g. before a ref to it has been attached);
the Grid then renders the rows at its top.

text:
Renders tabular data with virtualization along the vertical and horizontal axes.
Row heights and column widths must be known ahead of time and specified as properties.
 Scrolling is done through the imperative handle (ref): see scrollToCell and scrollToPosition.
title: Grid component props

text: The scrollToCell method ensures that a row and/or column is visible, scrolling the grid if necessary. Call it through a ref to the grid. Enter a row and column index below and click "Scroll": By default ("auto"), the grid scrolls the least amount possible to make the cell fully visible. Use the align parameter to align the cell to the "start" (top/left), "center", or "end" (bottom/right) of the grid instead. Pass only a rowIndex (or only a columnIndex) to scroll in one direction. scrollToCell is a one-time scroll: the grid doesn't remember the cell, so it isn't kept in view if the grid's size, its cell sizes or its row and column counts change afterwards. To scroll to a cell that is being added, call scrollToCell once the grid has rendered it (e.g. in an effect). Cells that haven't been measured yet (e.g. by CellMeasurer) are positioned using their estimated sizes. Use scrollToPosition to scroll to specific offsets instead. In version 10, the scrollToRow, scrollToColumn, scrollToAlignment, scrollTop and scrollLeft props were replaced by the scrollToCell and scrollToPosition methods. The autoHeight, autoWidth and isScrolling props were removed as well: to scroll a Grid with the window, set its scrollElement prop to "window", in which case scrollToCell and scrollToPosition scroll the window (vertically).
title: Scrolling to a cell

text: Row heights and column widths must be known ahead of time, but they don't all need to be the same. Instead of a number, rowHeight and columnWidth can be functions that return the size of a row or column given its index. The example below renders 1,000 rows and 1,000 columns with variable column widths and (optionally) variable row heights: Use variable row heights When sizes are functions, also specify estimatedRowSize and/or estimatedColumnSize. Cells are only measured as they are rendered, so these estimates are used to calculate the total size of the grid (and the size of its scrollbars) before all of its cells have been measured, which makes scrolling more consistent. Grid has no way of knowing when the data behind a rowHeight or columnWidth function changes. If sizes change, call the recomputeGridSize method. For sizes that depend on the rendered content, see CellMeasurer; to calculate column widths from the available width, see ColumnSizer.
title: Variable row and column sizes

headings.title: Forked styles
headings.text: Forked styles Copy the react-virtualized styles.css file into your project and load your own, totally custom version of it instead of the default one.

headings.title: Global CSS
headings.text: Global CSS Load an additional stylesheet (after the default one) that overrides or adds to the global class names that react-virtualized components render with. For example: The following global class names are used: Grid ReactVirtualized__Grid ReactVirtualized__Grid__innerScrollContainer List ReactVirtualized__List Table ReactVirtualized__Table ReactVirtualized__Table__Grid ReactVirtualized__Table__headerRow ReactVirtualized__Table__headerColumn ReactVirtualized__Table__headerTruncatedText ReactVirtualized__Table__sortableHeaderColumn ReactVirtualized__Table__sortableHeaderIcon ReactVirtualized__Table__sortableHeaderIcon--ASC ReactVirtualized__Table__sortableHeaderIcon--DESC ReactVirtualized__Table__row ReactVirtualized__Table__rowColumn Masonry ReactVirtualized__Masonry ReactVirtualized__Masonry__innerScrollContainer

headings.title: Custom class names
headings.text: Custom class names Components also accept custom class names, which are added alongside the default ones. For example Table supports className, gridClassName, headerClassName, and rowClassName (which can also be a function of the row index), and Column supports className and headerClassName. These work well with utility CSS frameworks; the table below is styled with Tailwind CSS classes: They also work well with CSS modules:

headings.title: Inline styles
headings.text: Inline styles Components also support inline style props for style overrides (e.g. Table supports style, gridStyle, headerStyle, and rowStyle): See the props pages (e.g. List props, Grid props, Table props, and Column props) to learn which class name and style props each component supports.

text: react-virtualized components position their rows and cells using inline styles, but the rest of their default appearance is defined in a separate stylesheet. Keeping these styles in their own file simplifies universal (server-side rendered) usage while also allowing them to be customized. This stylesheet should be imported once, usually while bootstrapping your application: The default stylesheet is small. Most of it is for Table (laying out header and row columns, truncating header text, and the sort indicator). List, Grid, and the other components work without it. Component styles can be customized in any of the ways below.
title: Customizing styles

text: The InfiniteLoader component was created to help break large data sets down into chunks that can be just-in-time loaded as they are scrolled into view. It can also be used to create an infinite-loading list (like a social media feed), where the total number of items isn't known up front and more items are loaded as the user reaches the end of the list. The trick is to render one extra row at the end of the list (as long as there are more items to load) to hold a loading indicator. That row is the only one that is not "loaded", so when it scrolls into view (or within InfiniteLoader's threshold), InfiniteLoader asks for the next page to be loaded. Here's a basic example of how you might implement that: The component above doesn't care where its data comes from. The demo on this page manages it with React state and simulates a network request for each page of items: Only one page is loaded at a time: while a page is loading, loadMoreRows is a no-op, in case InfiniteLoader asks for more rows to be loaded more than once.
title: Infinite-loading lists

headings.title: How it works
headings.text: How it works createTableMultiSort is passed a callback function, which it calls whenever the sort criteria change. It returns an object with three properties: sort: a function to pass to the Table sort prop; it updates the sort criteria in response to header clicks. sortBy: an ordered array of the fields data is sorted by, in order of importance. sortDirection: a map of field name to its sort direction ("ASC" or "DESC"). Because the Table sortBy and sortDirection props only describe a single column, they should be left undefined. Instead, use a custom headerRenderer to show a SortIndicator for each of the sorted columns: New sortBy and sortDirection values are created each time the sort criteria change (previous values are never mutated), so they can be stored in React state as they are. In version 9, they were mutated in place and had to be copied first.

headings.title: Default sort criteria
headings.text: Default sort criteria createTableMultiSort also accepts default sort-by values. Fields without a default direction are sorted in ascending order.

text: By default, Table assumes that its data will be sorted by a single attribute, in either ascending or descending order. For advanced use cases, you may want to sort by multiple fields. This can be accomplished using the createTableMultiSort utility. Try it out in the table above: Click a column header to sort by that column only (or to reverse its sort direction). SHIFT + click a column header to add it to the existing sort criteria (or to reverse its direction if it is already included). CONTROL + click (or META + click) a column header to remove it from the sort criteria.
title: Multi-column sort tables

text: By default, Table assumes that sortable rows can be sorted in ascending or descending order. Clicking a column header the first time calls the sort callback with a suggested ordering of ascending. Clicking it a second time suggests descending, and clicking a third time suggests ascending again. This is often desirable, but it has a subtle side effect: once a Table has been sorted, there is no way to return to the unsorted, “natural” order. Fortunately this is easy to implement in your application code. In the table below, clicking a column header a third time returns the rows to their natural order: Rather than always applying the suggested direction, the sort callback checks whether the table was already sorted in descending order by the clicked column. If it was, it clears the sort state (so that sortBy and sortDirection are undefined) and the unsorted list is rendered: See sorting for more about how Table sorting works.
title: Natural sort tables

text: Sometimes it is desirable to display a list in reverse order, with the newest items at the top (like a feed of incoming messages). The simplest way to do this is to add new items to the front of the array (like unshift) instead of the end (like push). The List below has a new item added to it every half second: Pause new items Here is a template for doing this. It also shows how to scroll back to the top of the list (using the scrollToRow method) when new items are added:
title: Displaying items in reverse order

headings.title: Sizes
headings.text: Sizes List, Grid, and Table need a height and width to know how many rows to render. AutoSizer can't measure anything on the server, so the sizes it provides are undefined there (and during hydration). Render with fallback sizes until it has measured the available space; otherwise nothing is rendered on the server: Once the page is hydrated, AutoSizer measures the available space and the list re-renders at its actual size. A component with a scrollElement uses its height prop the same way: as the height of the viewport until the scroll element has been measured.

headings.title: Rendering at an initial scroll position
headings.text: Rendering at an initial scroll position To render a list scrolled to a position (e.g. one restored from the URL when the user navigates back), use the initialScrollTop prop (and initialScrollLeft for a Grid or MultiGrid). The rows at that offset are rendered on the server, and the list is scrolled to it when it mounts: For example, this list is rendered scrolled to row 500 (an initialScrollTop of 15,000 pixels): The browser can't scroll an element before the page has been hydrated, so until then the server-rendered rows are shifted into view instead. After hydration the list is scrolled to the offset, and the rows stay in place. (Until then the scrollbar is shown at the top; if the user scrolls before the page has been hydrated, the rows they see stay in place as well.) Use initialScrollTop rather than calling scrollToRow in an effect: the effect only runs after hydration, so the page would first show the top of the list and then jump. Changing initialScrollTop after mounting has no effect; use scrollToPosition or scrollToRow to scroll a list that has already been rendered.

headings.title: Measured content
headings.text: Measured content CellMeasurer can only measure cells in the browser, so on the server (and during hydration) rows are rendered at the cache's default sizes, and they are re-positioned once they have been measured. Choose default sizes close to the typical size of your content to minimize the shift.

headings.title: Limitations
headings.text: Limitations A component with a scrollElement is rendered from its top on the server, using its height prop as the height of the viewport; once hydrated, it renders the rows visible within the scroll element (e.g. the window). Its vertical position is determined by the scroll element, so initialScrollTop doesn't apply. Masonry doesn't support an initial scroll offset: cell positions are only known once the cells before them have been measured, which can't happen on the server. The scrollbar size is measured after hydration, so the space reserved for scrollbars may change slightly at that point.

text: react-virtualized components can be rendered on the server (e.g. with renderToString or a framework like Next.js) and hydrated on the client. The server renders the rows (or cells) that would be visible, so the page shows content before JavaScript has loaded. This guide covers the things to keep in mind.
title: Server rendering

headings.title: Filling the available space
headings.text: Filling the available space In the example below, the list fills its container. Drag the bottom edge of the container to resize it; the list will resize to match. Grid and Table work the same way:

headings.title: Why are width and height undefined?
headings.text: Why are width and height undefined? AutoSizer can't know how much space is available until it has been mounted and has measured its parent, so the sizes are undefined during the first render. react-virtualized components require numbers, so render nothing (or a placeholder) until the values are defined. This can be done inside of a renderProp (as the other examples on this page do) or by passing a ChildComponent:

headings.title: Why is my AutoSizer setting a height of 0?
headings.text: Why is my AutoSizer setting a height of 0? AutoSizer expands to fill its parent but it will not stretch the parent. If AutoSizer is reporting a height (or width) of 0, then it's likely that the parent element (or one of its parents) has a height of 0. One easy way to test this is to temporarily add a style to the parent (e.g. background-color: red) to check that it is the size you expect. You may need to add height: 100% or flex: 1 to the parent.

headings.title: Can I use AutoSizer to manage only width or height (not both)?
headings.text: Can I use AutoSizer to manage only width or height (not both)? Yes. Only use the dimension you need, and only wait for that one to be defined. For example, a fixed-height list that grows to fill the available width can be created like so: A component that is scrolled by the window (with the scrollElement prop) only needs the width, too: its height is that of the window's viewport.

headings.title: Can I use AutoSizer within a flex container?
headings.text: Can I use AutoSizer within a flex container? AutoSizer measures its parent element, so when the space to fill is a flex item, wrap AutoSizer in a div that grows to fill that space. Also set min-height: 0 and min-width: 0 on that div; otherwise flex items can't shrink below the size of their content (the list), so the list would grow but never shrink. Don't make AutoSizer's parent size itself to its content (e.g. height: auto or width: fit-content); the size it reports would then depend on the size of the list, and nothing would be rendered.

headings.title: Can I use AutoSizer with other HOCs like InfiniteLoader?
headings.text: Can I use AutoSizer with other HOCs like InfiniteLoader? Yes. AutoSizer can be used within other react-virtualized HOCs such as InfiniteLoader or ScrollSync like so: See the InfiniteLoader page for a live example of this.

headings.title: Responding to size changes
headings.text: Responding to size changes Use the onResize prop to be notified when the size changes, e.g. to clear a CellMeasurer cache when the width changes and text wraps differently. See react-virtualized-auto-sizer for its other props.

headings.title: Migrating from react-virtualized 9.x
headings.text: Migrating from react-virtualized 9.x Earlier versions of react-virtualized included an AutoSizer component. It has been removed in version 10. To migrate to react-virtualized-auto-sizer (version 2): Import AutoSizer from "react-virtualized-auto-sizer" rather than "react-virtualized". Replace the children render function with the renderProp prop (or with the ChildComponent prop; see below). Handle undefined sizes: width and height are undefined until the parent has been measured (including during server rendering). Remove disableHeight and disableWidth; just ignore the dimension that you don't need. Remove defaultHeight and defaultWidth; render a placeholder while the size is undefined instead.

text: Many react-virtualized components (e.g. List, Grid, and Table) require explicit pixel dimensions, but sometimes you just want a component to grow to fill all of the available space. The react-virtualized-auto-sizer package measures its parent element and passes the available width and height to its child. (A component that is scrolled by the window only needs a width; see below.) As of version 10, AutoSizer is no longer part of react-virtualized; use the react-virtualized-auto-sizer package instead. It works with all react-virtualized components (and with react-window). See migrating from react-virtualized 9.x below.
title: Sizing components

headings.title: Usage
headings.text: Usage InfiniteLoader uses a render function as its child. That function receives two parameters, which should be passed to the virtualized component it renders: onRowsRendered should be passed as the child's onRowsRendered prop. It informs the loader when the user is scrolling. registerChild should be set as the child's ref. It enables a set of rows to be refreshed once their data has finished loading. The isRowLoaded prop tells the loader which rows have already been loaded, and loadMoreRows is called to load rows that haven't been. loadMoreRows should return a Promise that resolves once the data has finished loading; it is used to determine when to refresh the list with the newly-loaded data. The number of rows to load at a time can be tuned with the minimumBatchSize prop (e.g. to reduce the number of HTTP requests), and how early rows are pre-fetched with the threshold prop. To build a list that loads more items as the user reaches its end (e.g. a feed), see infinite-loading lists.

headings.text: Using InfiniteLoader with Grid It is not common to use InfiniteLoader and Grid together but it is possible, by mapping the range of rendered cells to a range of "rows" (one per cell):

headings.title: Edge cases and considerations
headings.text: Edge cases and considerations Tracking loaded (and loading) rows InfiniteLoader is not a stateful component, meaning that it does not keep track of which rows it has requested to be loaded. Your component will need to track this information itself to avoid loading rows multiple times. One way to do this is to use a map to track the status of each row: rows with no entry have never been requested, and rows with an entry (either "loading" or "loaded") can be treated as loaded as far as InfiniteLoader is concerned. The demo at the top of this page does this: Memoization and data changes InfiniteLoader memoizes calls to loadMoreRows in order to avoid multiple calls with the same parameters while a user is scrolling. This can have an unexpected impact if the underlying data changes: InfiniteLoader may not know to call loadMoreRows again because, from its point of view, it already made that call for a given range of rows. (React Virtualized components know nothing about the underlying data, only the number of items in the collection.) To address this, call the resetLoadMoreRowsCache method (through a ref) when the underlying data may have changed, e.g. a filtered list whose search criteria changes. (Alternately, your application can call its own loadMoreRows function again with the most recently requested range.)

headings.text: Methods Imperative API exposed by InfiniteLoader (e.g. via useRef<InfiniteLoaderImperativeAPI>(null)).

headings.title: resetLoadMoreRowsCache
headings.text:
resetLoadMoreRowsCache Reset any cached data about already-loaded rows.
This method should be called if any/all loaded data needs to be refetched (e.g. a filtered list where the search criteria changes).
If autoReload is true, the last loaded batch will be automatically reloaded.

headings.title: children
headings.text:
Function responsible for rendering a virtualized component.
It is passed onRowsRendered and registerChild parameters.
The onRowsRendered function should be passed through to the child's onRowsRendered property.
The registerChild callback should be set as the virtualized component's ref.

headings.title: isRowLoaded
headings.text:
Function responsible for tracking the loaded state of each row.
Rows that are currently loading can be treated as loaded to avoid requesting them multiple times.

headings.title: loadMoreRows
headings.text:
Callback to be invoked when more rows must be loaded.
The returned Promise should be resolved once row data has finished loading.
It will be used to determine when to refresh the list with the newly-loaded data.
This callback may be called multiple times in reaction to a single scroll event.

headings.title: minimumBatchSize
headings.text:
Minimum number of rows to be loaded at a time.
This property can be used to batch requests to reduce HTTP requests.

headings.text: Number of rows in list; can be arbitrary high number if actual number is unknown.

headings.title: threshold
headings.text:
Threshold at which to pre-fetch data.
A threshold X means that data will start loading when a user scrolls within X rows.

text: InfiniteLoader manages just-in-time fetching of data as a user scrolls up or down in a list. It ensures that all visible rows have been loaded, and uses a threshold to determine how early to pre-fetch rows (before a user scrolls to them). This component is intended to assist with row-loading, so it is best suited for use with List and Table (although it can also be used with Grid). This is an advanced component and can be confusing in certain situations. See the edge cases and considerations section below for more information.
title: InfiniteLoader

headings.text: Empty lists Use the noRowsRenderer prop to render placeholder content when rowCount is 0:

text: List renders a windowed (or "virtualized") list of rows, meaning that only the rows visible within the list (plus a few overscanned rows) are rendered. This keeps the number of DOM elements small, no matter how many rows the list contains. To render a list, specify its size (width and height), how many rows it contains (rowCount), the height of each row (rowHeight), and a function that renders a row (rowRenderer; see rendering rows). Rows are rendered through a function, rather than as children, for performance reasons. The example above uses AutoSizer to fill the available space: List uses a Grid internally to render its rows, and all props are relayed to that inner Grid. That means List also accepts Grid props in addition to its own List props. By default List renders 10 extra rows above and below the visible ones (overscanRowCount), which can help reduce flickering during scrolling on certain browsers and devices. See overscan for an important note about this property. The outer element of a list has the static class name ReactVirtualized__List; a custom className, id, and style can be specified too. See customizing styles for more information.
title: Rendering a list

headings.title: forceUpdateGrid
headings.text:
forceUpdateGrid Forcefully re-render the inner Grid component.
Re-rendering a List with the same props does not re-render its rows (both List and the inner Grid are memoized).
Use this method if you want to manually trigger a re-render.
This may be appropriate if the underlying row data has changed but the row sizes themselves have not.

headings.title: getOffsetForRow
headings.text:
getOffsetForRow Gets the vertical offset (scrollTop) for a given row and alignment (see scrollToRow for the align values).
The alignment defaults to "auto"; an index of -1 (the default) refers to the last row.
alignment is a deprecated alias of align (align takes precedence if both are specified).

headings.title: invalidateCellSizeAfterRender
headings.text:
invalidateCellSizeAfterRender Invalidate the size of a row (after the current render has been committed); see Grid#invalidateCellSizeAfterRender.
This method is intended for CellMeasurer.

headings.title: measureAllRows
headings.text:
measureAllRows Pre-measure all rows in a List.
Typically rows are only measured as needed and estimated heights are used for cells that have not yet been measured.
This method ensures that the next call to getTotalSize() returns an exact size (as opposed to just an estimated one).

headings.title: recomputeRowHeights
headings.text:
recomputeRowHeights Recompute row heights and offsets after the specified index (defaults to 0).
List has no way of knowing when its underlying list data has changed since it only receives a rowHeight property.
If the rowHeight is a number it can compare before and after values but if it is a function that comparison is error prone.
In the event that a dynamic rowHeight function is in use and the row heights have changed this function should be manually called by the "smart" container parent.
This method will also force a render cycle (via forceUpdate) to ensure that the updated measurements are reflected in the rendered list.

headings.title: recomputeGridSize
headings.text:
recomputeGridSize Recompute row heights and offsets after the specified row index (defaults to 0); see Grid#recomputeGridSize.
(The column index is ignored.) This method is intended for CellMeasurer; also see recomputeRowHeights.

headings.title: scrollToCell
headings.text:
scrollToCell Ensure the specified row is visible (scrolling if necessary); the column index is ignored.
This allows a List to be used with ArrowKeyStepper; also see scrollToRow.

headings.title: scrollToPosition
headings.text:
scrollToPosition Scroll to the specified vertical offset; scrollLeft is ignored (lists don't scroll horizontally).
Offsets are clamped to the scrollable range. This allows a List to be used with ScrollSync.
Useful for animating position changes.
If the List has a scrollElement, the scroll element (e.g. the window) is scrolled instead.

headings.title: scrollToRow
headings.text:
scrollToRow Ensure the row at the specified index is visible (scrolling if necessary).
This method can be used to safely scroll back to a row that a user has scrolled away from even if it was previously scrolled to.
The align parameter (default "auto") controls the alignment of the row:
"auto" scrolls the least amount possible to ensure that the specified row is fully visible
(a row taller than the list is aligned to its start, so that its start is visible);
"start" aligns the row to the top of the list and "end" to the bottom; "center" aligns it in the middle.
This is a one-time scroll: the row is not kept in view afterwards (e.g. if the list's size or its row heights change).
Rows that haven't been measured yet (e.g. by CellMeasurer) are positioned using their estimated heights.
If the List has a scrollElement, the scroll element (e.g. the window) is scrolled instead.

headings.title: Calling methods
headings.text: Calling methods List's methods can be called through a ref. The example below uses scrollToRow to scroll the list. In version 10, these methods replace the scrollToIndex, scrollToAlignment and scrollTop props; see scrolling to a row: To compute the offset of a row without scrolling to it, use getOffsetForRow; it accepts the same align parameter as scrollToRow (e.g. getOffsetForRow({ align: "center", index: 500 })). The alignment parameter of earlier versions is deprecated but still supported.

headings.text: Recomputing row heights When a rowHeight function is used and the data behind it changes, call recomputeRowHeights so that the list re-measures its rows:

headings.title: rowCount
headings.text: Number of rows in list.

headings.title: rowHeight
headings.text:
Either a fixed row height (number) or a function that returns the height of a row given its index: ({ index: number }): number.
If function is used, specify estimatedRowSize for more consistent scrolling behavior.

headings.title: rowRenderer
headings.text:
Responsible for rendering a row given its index.
It receives index, isScrolling, isVisible, key, parent, and style parameters.
 The style parameter specifies how the row is to be sized and positioned and must be passed through to the rendered row element.
The key parameter must also be applied to the rendered element.

headings.title: width
headings.text: Width of the list.

headings.title: aria-label
headings.text:
ARIA label for the list element. There is no default label.
(With role="grid", it defaults to "grid", as in version 9.)

headings.title: aria-readonly
headings.text:
ARIA readonly attribute for the list element.
Not set by default (it doesn't apply to role="list"); with role="grid", it defaults to true.

headings.title: cellRangeRenderer
headings.text:
Responsible for rendering a group of cells given their index ranges.
 This is an advanced property.
It is useful for situations where the Grid requires additional, overlayed UI (such as a Gantt chart or a calendar application).
The easiest way to override it is to decorate defaultCellRangeRenderer.
 Defaults to defaultCellRangeRenderer.

headings.text: Optional custom CSS class name to attach to root List element.

headings.title: containerProps
headings.text: Additional props (eg onWheel) to spread onto the outer Grid element.

headings.title: containerRole
headings.text:
ARIA role for the inner container of the rows.
Defaults to "presentation" (so that the rows belong to the list), or to "row" with role="grid".

headings.title: containerStyle
headings.text: Optional custom inline style to attach to inner cell-container element.

headings.title: deferredMeasurementCache
headings.text:
If CellMeasurer is used to measure this Grid's children, this should be a pointer to its CellMeasurerCache.
A shared CellMeasurerCache reference enables Grid and CellMeasurer to share measurement data.

headings.title: elementRef
headings.text: Reference to the outer (scrolling) DOM element.

headings.title: estimatedRowSize
headings.text:
Used to estimate the total height of a List before all of its rows have actually been measured.
The estimated total height is adjusted as rows are rendered.

headings.title: getScrollbarSize
headings.text:
Returns the size of the browser's scrollbar.
Exposed for testing purposes only.
 Defaults to measuring (and caching) the width of the browser's native scrollbar.

headings.title: height
headings.text:
Height constraint for list (determines how many actual rows are rendered).
Required, unless a scrollElement is specified.
 With a scrollElement, the height of the scroll element's viewport is used instead;
this prop is then only used until the scroll element has been measured (e.g. during server rendering).

headings.title: id
headings.text: Optional custom id to attach to root List element.

headings.title: initialScrollTop
headings.text:
Vertical scroll offset to initially render (and scroll to) the Grid at.
Only the initial value is used: changing this prop later has no effect (use scrollToPosition to scroll).
This also works with server rendering: the cells at this offset are rendered on the server,
and they stay in place when the page is hydrated.
Ignored if a scrollElement is specified (which then determines the vertical offset).

headings.title: isScrollingOptOut
headings.text:
Prevents re-rendering of visible cells on scroll end.
(Opts out of the isScrolling param passed to cellRangeRenderer, to avoid the extra render when scroll stops.)
Visible cells are still re-rendered when the Grid's props change or forceUpdate() is called.

headings.title: noRowsRenderer
headings.text:
Callback used to render placeholder content when rowCount is 0.
By default, nothing is rendered.

headings.title: onRowsRendered
headings.text:
Callback invoked with information about the slice of rows that were just rendered:
({ overscanStartIndex: number, overscanStopIndex: number, startIndex: number, stopIndex: number }): void.

headings.title: onScroll
headings.text:
Callback invoked whenever the scroll offset changes within the inner scrollable region:
({ clientHeight: number, scrollHeight: number, scrollTop: number }): void.
This callback can be used to sync scrolling between lists, tables, or grids.

headings.title: onScrollbarPresenceChange
headings.text:
Called whenever a horizontal or vertical scrollbar is added or removed:
({ horizontal: boolean, size: number, vertical: boolean }): void.
This prop is not intended for end-user use;
it is used by MultiGrid to support fixed-row/fixed-column scroll syncing.

headings.title: overscanIndicesGetter
headings.text:
Responsible for calculating the number of rows to overscan before and after a specified range.
By default (accessibilityOverscanIndicesGetter), at least one row is overscanned in each direction (for accessibility).
See Grid overscanIndicesGetter for details.

headings.title: overscanRowCount
headings.text:
Number of rows to render above/below the visible bounds of the list.
This can help reduce flickering during scrolling on certain browsers/devices.
 Note that this property has performance implications: the higher the value, the more work needs to be done in reaction to each scroll event.

headings.title: role
headings.text:
ARIA role for the list element.
With the default "list", rows that don't specify a role get role="listitem" (#1657).
Pass "grid" for the version 9 roles (a grid element whose rows are gridcells within a single row).

headings.title: scrollElement
headings.text:
Element that scrolls the List (instead of the List scrolling itself): "window", or a scrollable DOM element
(e.g. a container that the List is rendered within, along with other content).
 The List then renders at its full height, renders only the rows visible within the scroll element's viewport,
and its scroll methods scroll the scroll element.
Its position within the scroll element is measured when the scroll element scrolls or is resized, and when the List re-renders
(e.g. call forceUpdateGrid() if content above the List changes size without the List re-rendering).
Pass null while the scroll element isn't available yet (e.g. before a ref to it has been attached);
the List then renders the rows at its top.

headings.title: scrollingResetTimeInterval
headings.text: Wait this amount of time (in milliseconds) after the last scroll event before resetting Grid pointer-events.

headings.title: style
headings.text: Optional custom inline style to attach to root List element.

headings.title: tabIndex
headings.text: Optional override of tab index default.

text:
It is inefficient to create and manage a large list of DOM elements within a scrolling container
if only a few of those elements are visible. The primary purpose of this component is to improve
performance by only rendering the DOM nodes that a user is able to see based on their current
scroll position.
 This component renders a virtualized list of elements with either fixed or dynamic heights.
title: List component props

headings.title: Scrolling placeholders
headings.text: Scrolling placeholders If row content is expensive to render, consider rendering a light-weight placeholder while the list is being scrolled. The isScrolling parameter passed to rowRenderer makes this possible:

text: The rowRenderer function is responsible for rendering a single row, given its index. It must return an element that applies the style parameter (which positions and sizes the row) and has a unique key, and whose content fits within the row's height: It is very important that rows do not have vertical overflow. Overflow would make scrolling the list difficult (as individual rows would intercept the scroll events). For this reason it is recommended that rows use a style like overflow-y: hidden.
title: Rendering rows

text: The scrollToRow method ensures that a row is visible, scrolling the list if necessary. Call it through a ref to the list. By default ("auto") the list scrolls the least amount possible to make the row fully visible (a row taller than the list is scrolled to its start); use the align parameter to align the row to the "start", "center", or "end" of the list instead. scrollToRow is a one-time scroll: the list doesn't remember the row, so it isn't kept in view if the list's size, its row heights or its row count change afterwards. To scroll to a row that is being added, call scrollToRow once the list has rendered it (e.g. in an effect). Rows that haven't been measured yet (e.g. by CellMeasurer) are positioned using their estimated heights. In version 10, the scrollToIndex, scrollToAlignment and scrollTop props were replaced by the scrollToRow and scrollToPosition methods, and the autoHeight and isScrolling props were removed: to scroll a List with the window, set its scrollElement prop to "window", in which case scrollToRow scrolls the window. The same applies to Table.
title: Scrolling to a row

text: Rows don't all need to be the same height. Instead of a number, rowHeight can be a function that returns the height of a row given its index. In that case, also specify an estimatedRowSize; it is used to estimate the total height of the list before all of its rows have been measured, which makes scrolling more consistent. List has no way of knowing when the data behind a rowHeight function changes. If row heights change, call the recomputeRowHeights method. For row heights that depend on the rendered content, see CellMeasurer.
title: Variable row heights

text: Masonry efficiently displays dynamically-sized, user-positioned cells using windowing techniques. Cells are measured just-in-time and laid out as the user scrolls. Sizes are cached so that resizing (and re-flowing) the layout is fast and does not require re-measuring. Cell positions are controlled by an injected cellPositioner prop. Windowing is vertical; Masonry does not support horizontal scrolling. 200px columns 10px gutter A Masonry requires a CellMeasurerCache (to measure and cache the size of each cell), a cell positioner (to lay out the measured cells), and a cellRenderer that wraps each cell in a CellMeasurer: The style passed to cellRenderer positions the cell, so it must be passed through to the rendered element. The parent parameter is the Masonry's imperative handle and should be passed to CellMeasurer. See the props page for the full list of supported props, and measuring and layout for how (and with which constraints) cells are measured and positioned. Masonry renders the following static class names, which can be used for styling: ReactVirtualized__Masonry: main (outer) element ReactVirtualized__Masonry__innerScrollContainer: inner scrollable area
title: Rendering a masonry layout

headings.title: createMasonryCellPositioner
headings.text: createMasonryCellPositioner Masonry provides a built-in positioner, createMasonryCellPositioner, for a simple column layout. It places each cell into the column that is currently the shortest. It requires a few configuration settings:

headings.title: Updating the layout
headings.text: Updating the layout If any of these settings change due to external changes (eg a window resize event), update them using the positioner's reset method and then tell Masonry to re-position its cells using recomputeCellPositions() : Unlike createMasonryCellPositioner, reset does not default spacer to 0; always specify it.

headings.title: Custom positioners
headings.text: Custom positioners Custom layouts can be implemented with a custom positioner. Because the positioner tracks layout state as it goes (eg the height of each column), it needs a way to be reset before Masonry re-positions its cells:

text: A cell positioner is a function that is given a cell index and returns the cell's position: (index) => ({ left, top }). It is called in index order, once for each cell, after that cell has been measured; so it can read the cell's height (and the heights of all earlier cells) from the CellMeasurerCache. The positions it returns are cached by Masonry.
title: Cell positioners

text: Masonry layouts are often used to display images. Because cell measurements must be synchronous, the size of each image must be known before its cell is rendered (eg by setting an explicit height and width on the , using dimensions provided by the server). Otherwise the cell would be measured before the image loads, and the measurement would be wrong. In the basic example, colored blocks with a known height stand in for images; an image with known dimensions works the same way. Scale the height to the column width to preserve the image's aspect ratio, eg columnWidth * (imageHeight / imageWidth). Items can only be measured once; measurements are cached permanently (until the cache is cleared). If image sizes aren't known up front (eg the server can't provide them), they need to be pre-measured before they are passed to Masonry. To preserve a correct layout, images can only be displayed one by one in the order they appear in the list (not in the order they finish loading). The react-virtualized-image-measurer library handles this; it loads the images, then passes each item along with its size to a render function that renders the Masonry (live demo).
title: Images

headings.title: Layout constraints
headings.text: Layout constraints Multi-column layouts are supported. Each cell can have a unique, lazily-measured height. Cells may not span multiple columns: the width of all cells in a column should be equal (and must not exceed the column's width), and the left position of all cells within a column must align. Cell measurements must be synchronous. A cell's size impacts the layout, and asynchronous measurements would require frequent layout invalidation. The asynchronous measure function passed to CellMeasurer's render callback is not supported by Masonry. (See images for how to handle content such as images whose size isn't known up front.)

headings.title: Animation constraints
headings.text: Animation constraints Simple animations are supported (eg translating or sliding cells into place when they are first revealed). More complex animations are not (eg cells flying from one position to another on resize).

text: Rendering occurs in two phases: Measurement: Estimated cell sizes (the defaultHeight and defaultWidth of the cellMeasurerCache) are used to decide how many cells to measure in a batch. The batch size is chosen using a fast, naive layout algorithm that stacks cells in order until the viewport has been filled. After measurement is complete, Masonry evaluates the positioned cells to determine whether another measurement pass is required (eg if actual cell sizes were smaller than the estimated sizes). All measurements are permanently cached (keyed by keyMapper) for performance purposes. Layout: The external cellPositioner is used to position cells. At this point the positioner has access to cached size measurements for all of the cells it is asked to position. The positions it returns are cached by Masonry for fast access later. The measurement phase is repeated if the user scrolls beyond the bounds of the current layout. If the layout is invalidated (eg due to a resize), cached positions can be cleared using recomputeCellPositions() or clearCellPositions() . By default, measurements and positions are cached by index. If cells can be re-ordered (or inserted), provide a keyMapper that maps an index to a unique id, and use the same mapping for the CellMeasurerCache's keyMapper, so that cached measurements aren't associated with the wrong cells.
title: Measuring and layout

headings.title: clearCellPositions
headings.text:
clearCellPositions Clears the internal position cache and re-renders.
Cells are positioned again (by the cellPositioner) as they are rendered.

headings.title: forceUpdate
headings.text:
forceUpdate Forcefully re-renders the Masonry (and its visible cells).
Re-rendering a Masonry with the same props does not re-render its cells (it is memoized).
Use this method if the underlying cell data has changed but the props have not.

headings.title: invalidateCellSizeAfterRender
headings.text:
invalidateCellSizeAfterRender Notifies the Masonry that the specified cell has been measured for the first time (while rendering);
the cell is positioned (by the cellPositioner) once the current render has been committed, then the Masonry re-renders.
Only rowIndex (the cell's index) is used.
This method is intended for CellMeasurer.

headings.title: recomputeCellPositions
headings.text:
recomputeCellPositions Resets the internal position cache, synchronously re-computes the positions of all measured cells
(by calling the cellPositioner for each of them, in index order), then re-renders.
Reset the cellPositioner (e.g. with its reset method) before calling this method.

headings.title: recomputeGridSize
headings.text:
recomputeGridSize Re-renders the Masonry, e.g. after more cells have been loaded (this method is called by InfiniteLoader)
or a cell has been re-measured (it is called by CellMeasurer's measure function).
Parameters (the index of the first changed cell, as rowIndex) are accepted for compatibility with Grid and ignored.
Cached cell positions are not changed: to re-position cells after their sizes have changed,
reset the cellPositioner and call recomputeCellPositions().

headings.title: Usage
headings.text: Usage Masonry exposes these methods through an imperative handle, which can be accessed using a ref (eg useRef<MasonryImperativeAPI>(null)). The cell positioning methods are typically called after updating the cell positioner, eg when the container is resized: recomputeCellPositions() synchronously re-positions every cell that has already been measured, using cached measurements. Use it when the layout changes but cell sizes don't (eg the number of columns or the space between them). clearCellPositions() discards cached positions; cells are positioned again only as they are measured. If cell sizes have changed too (eg the column width changed, so text wraps differently), clear the CellMeasurerCache (cache.clearAll()) before calling it, otherwise cells that were already measured won't be re-positioned. invalidateCellSizeAfterRender and recomputeGridSize are called by CellMeasurer (through the parent passed to cellRenderer, which is this handle) and by InfiniteLoader (to re-render cells once they have loaded); they don't need to be called directly.

text:
Imperative API of a Masonry (accessed using a ref, eg useRef<MasonryImperativeAPI>(null)).
This is also the parent value passed to cellRenderer (for CellMeasurer).

headings.text: Total number of items.

headings.title: cellMeasurerCache
headings.text:
Caches item measurements (typically an instance of CellMeasurerCache).
Default sizes help Masonry decide how many images to batch-measure.

headings.title: cellPositioner
headings.text:
Positions a cell given an index: (index: number) => ({ left: number, top: number }).
See createMasonryCellPositioner for a built-in positioner.

headings.title: cellRenderer
headings.text:
Responsible for rendering a cell given an index:
({ index: number, isScrolling: boolean, key: Key, parent: MasonryImperativeAPI, style: CSSProperties }) => ReactNode.
The style param must be passed through to the rendered cell element.
The cell should typically be wrapped in a CellMeasurer.

headings.title: width
headings.text: Width of the component; this value determines the number of visible items.

headings.title: aria-label
headings.text: Optional ARIA label to attach to root Masonry element.

headings.title: className
headings.text: Optional custom CSS class name to attach to root Masonry element.

headings.title: height
headings.text:
Height of the component; this value determines the number of visible items.
Required, unless a scrollElement is specified.
 With a scrollElement, the height of the scroll element's viewport is used instead;
this prop is then only used until the scroll element has been measured (e.g. during server rendering).

headings.title: id
headings.text: Optional custom id to attach to root Masonry element.

headings.title: keyMapper
headings.text:
Maps an index to a unique id to store cached measurement and position info for a cell.
This prevents eg cached measurements from being invalidated when a collection is re-ordered.
Defaults to the identity function (index => index).

headings.title: onCellsRendered
headings.text:
Callback invoked with information about the cells that were most recently rendered.
This callback is only invoked when visible cells have changed:
({ startIndex: number, stopIndex: number }): void.
Does nothing by default.

headings.title: onScroll
headings.text:
Callback invoked whenever the scroll offset changes within the inner scrollable region:
({ clientHeight: number, scrollHeight: number, scrollTop: number }): void.
Does nothing by default.

headings.title: overscanByPixels
headings.text:
Render this many additional pixels above and below the viewport.
This helps reduce flicker when a user scrolls quickly.

headings.title: scrollElement
headings.text:
Element that scrolls the Masonry (instead of the Masonry scrolling itself): "window", or a scrollable DOM element
(e.g. a container that the Masonry is rendered within, along with other content).
 The Masonry then renders at its full height, and renders only the cells visible within the scroll element's viewport.
Its position within the scroll element is measured when the scroll element scrolls or is resized, and when the Masonry re-renders
(e.g. call forceUpdate() if content above the Masonry changes size without the Masonry re-rendering).
Pass null while the scroll element isn't available yet (e.g. before a ref to it has been attached);
the Masonry then renders the cells at its top.
